item.title: A taste of Italy: Alessandro Giannatempo’s recipes for Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, and crocodile’s porridge
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: rich in cultural context and diverse ingredients, with detailed recipe instructions

Although I grew up in Emilia-Romagna, my family history spans the Italian peninsula. Inspired by my mixed upbringing, these recipes reflect the flavours of both southern and northern Italy. The Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, as the name suggests, is a nod to the southern coast of Salerno. Fresh ricotta is whipped with lemony pears and sandwiched between layers of nutty hazelnut cake. The crocodile’s porridge, named after a traditional Italian beverage made with milk and pear juice, combines northern ingredients such as polenta and amaro for a very cosy stovetop-made dessert – or breakfast, if you ask me!

Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake

Prep 15 min

Cook 1 hr 30 min

Chill 6 hr+

Serves 10-14

For the cake

200g whole shelled hazelnuts

70g cornflour

3 large eggs

100g granulated sugar

½ tsp fine sea salt

70g vegetable oil

½ tsp baking powder

For the poached pears

500g peeled, cored and diced conference pears (about 5 medium-small pears)

70g granulated sugar

1 unwaxed lemon, zest peeled off in strips, and the fruit juiced

For the ricotta filling

500g ricotta

70g granulated sugar

300g double cream

To serve

15-20g icing sugar

Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and roast the hazelnuts for 10-15 minutes, until browned. Remove, and leave the oven on.

While the hazelnuts are still hot, wrap them in a clean tea towel, leave to steam for five minutes, then rub off the skins. Leave to cool completely, then blitz the hazelnuts and the cornflour in a food processor to a medium-fine texture (like ground coffee), using short, quick pulses to avoid overheating the mix.

Grease the base of a 20cm cake tin that’s at least 8cm tall, then line it with greaseproof paper.

Using a stand mixer or electric whisk, whip the eggs, sugar and salt on medium-high for four to five minutes, until pale and tripled in volume. With the motor still running, slowly stream in the oil until emulsified.

In a separate medium bowl, combine the hazelnut mix and baking powder. Whisk in a few tablespoons of the whipped eggs, then gently incorporate the rest of the egg mix in three stages. Pour the batter into the lined tin and bake for 25-30 minutes, or until golden and springy, and a toothpick inserted into the centre comes out clean. Remove from the oven and leave the cake in its tin until completely cool.

Meanwhile, in a small saucepan, bring the diced pears, 90ml water, sugar, lemon juice and peel to a boil on a medium-high heat, then cook for eight to 10 minutes, until tender but still slightly firm. Leave to cool, then strain, reserving the cooking liquid.

Remove the cake from its tin and use a serrated knife to cut it in half horizontally. Brush the exposed side of each half with the reserved pear liquid.

Whisk the ricotta and sugar for one to two minutes. Whip the cream to soft peaks, then add the ricotta mix and whip again to firm peaks. Fold in the poached pear pieces.

Line the cake tin with clingfilm, leaving plenty of overhang. Put one cake layer in the tin, crumb side up. Spoon in the ricotta mixture, then put the second cake crumb side down on top. Wrap tightly and refrigerate for at least six hours, and preferably overnight.

When you’re ready to serve, unmould the cake, dust it with icing sugar, slice and serve. Buon appetito! The cake will keep well wrapped and in the fridge for up to five days.

Crocodile’s porridge

Prep 10 min

Cook 1 hr, plus cooling

Serves 4

For the polenta porridge

100g polenta bramata, or other coarsely ground yellow cornmeal

¼ tsp fine sea salt

770g whole milk

30g cold unsalted butter

For the buttered almonds

60g sliced almonds

20g granulated sugar

1 pinch fine sea salt

20g unsalted butter

For the amaro-poached pears

80g granulated sugar

250g amaro

Juice of 1 lemon

1 pinch fine sea salt

3 medium-small conference pears

In a bowl, combine the polenta, salt and milk, then set aside. This step will help the polenta hydrate and cuts down on the cooking time.

Meanwhile, in a medium-sized, heavy-bottomed pot on a medium heat, toast the sliced almonds until fragrant and blond. Move the pan off the heat, then stir in the sugar and salt, and let them melt. Add the butter, stir to combine, then tip on to a plate to cool.

In the same pan, bring 80g sugar, the amaro, 250ml cold water, lemon juice and a pinch of salt to a boil. In the meantime, peel, core and slice each pear into four lengthways. Add the pear pieces to the pot, lower the heat, cover with a cartouche (a round sheet of baking paper) and simmer gently for 20 minutes, until the pears are just tender when pricked with a skewer. Turn off the heat and leave the fruit to cool for 10-15 minutes. Transfer the pears and 60g of their poaching liquid into a clean bowl, cover and set aside.

Add the milk and polenta mix to the pear poaching liquid left in the pan and turn on the heat to medium. Once boiling, cook for 10 minutes, whisking constantly, until the mix turns creamy and slightly thicker; the whisking is essential here – we’re making polenta, after all. Stir in the cold butter to melt.

Serve the warm sweet polenta topped with the poached pears and a sprinkling of buttered almonds, spoon over the poaching liquid and buon appetito!

- Alessandro Giannatempo is a London-based pastry chef and recipe writer.

item.title: Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: useful for learning about meal kits and specific recipe preparation, but lacks depth in cultural context

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested—and re-tested—just about every meal delivery service. Each time we try HelloFresh, we're impressed by its bold flavors, so we teamed up with the brand to bring you our favorite recipes each week (read more about how we chose them here). Sign up for a delivery, and you also get a 3-month digital subscription to BA for free. Here's a closer look at one of our BA Picks.

Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I'm tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh's Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

What it is

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn's glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

What's in the box

You'll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

How it came together

True to the recipe card's promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan's heat. I don't often cook shrimp at home, and was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

How it tastes

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there's a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

Who it's for

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredients' list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

The bottom line

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table quickly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It's tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.
